readerTitle: The best cook isn't always the right chef
caseNote: 가상 사례 (도시락·간편식 생산 주방, 클리닉용 예약 소프트웨어 회사) + 실제 관찰 (주방 채용에서 흔한 시범 근무 관행) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 좋은 후보를 고르는 일은 '누가 더 뛰어난가'가 아니라 '이 자리가 1년 안에 무엇을 해내야 하는가'를 먼저 적고, 그 일을 직접 해보게 하는 것에서 시작한다.
misconception: 가장 실력 좋고 이력이 화려한 사람을 뽑으면 어느 자리든 잘 해낸다. 대표 요리를 맛보면 셰프의 실력을 알 수 있다.

sources.text: PPL-03-01 (역할 정의), PPL-03-03 (실제 업무 능력 테스트) 개념 레슨을 적용
모든 인물, 회사, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 하루 2,000식, 조리 인력 8명, 오전 5시 시작, 식재료 원가 목표 30%는 모두 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 30%는 외식·식품 업계에서 흔히 언급되는 범위 안의 값으로 골랐지만 특정 출처의 통계로 제시하지 않았습니다.
주방 채용에서 짧은 시범 근무(trial shift, 'stage')를 하는 관행은 업계에서 널리 관찰되는 일반적 사실로만 언급했습니다. 특정 비율이나 연구 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다.
무급 시범 근무의 적법성은 나라와 지역마다 다릅니다. 법률 조언을 피하기 위해 6번 카드에서는 '유급으로 짧게, 지역 규칙 확인'이라는 일반 원칙만 적었습니다.

cards.title: The best cook isn't always the right chef
body: Mira's kitchen makes 2,000 ready meals a day for cafés and offices. Her head chef just quit.

Two applicants stand out. One ran a well-reviewed restaurant. The other was a sous-chef in a hotel banquet kitchen. The restaurant chef's food is clearly better. That may not decide who is better at *this* job.

image.label: Two chefs standing outside a large production kitchen
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 고급 접시를 든 셰프, 오른쪽에 대형 냄비와 클립보드를 든 셰프. 뒤로 컨베이어와 포장 용기가 늘어선 대형 생산 주방. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: Where do you start?
body: Both chefs want the job, and you have one week to decide. What is your first move?

options.text: Interview both and go with the stronger reputation
options.feedback: Reputation is fast to judge, but it was earned in other jobs. You'd be comparing them to a vague idea of 'a great chef', not to your kitchen.

options.text: Write down what the head chef must deliver in year one, then compare
options.feedback: This is **defining the role**. It takes an hour, and it tells you which strengths matter here and what to test next.

options.text: Ask each to cook a signature dish for you
options.feedback: You'll learn about taste and technique. But a signature dish shows the restaurant job, not a 2,000-meal production line.

cards.title: What the job actually is
body: Mira lists what the new head chef must deliver in the first year. None of it says "cook a beautiful plate."

breakdown.label: Food cost target
breakdown.detail: Every recipe costed before it ships

cards.callout: Now the banquet sous-chef's big-batch experience counts for more, and plating counts for less. Neither chef is ruled out. Mira just knows what to test.

cards.title: Design the tryout
body: Mira wants to see each chef work before deciding. Which tryout tells her the most?

options.text: A tasting: each chef cooks three dishes of their choice
options.feedback: It shows real cooking skill, but it tests what each chef chose to show, not the four outcomes on Mira's list.

options.text: A paid half-day: scale a real recipe to 400 portions, cost it, brief two cooks
options.feedback: This is **testing real skills**. The task is a slice of the real job, so it checks consistency, costing and leadership directly.

options.text: A long interview on food safety, scheduling and costs
options.feedback: Good questions, and useful later. But talking about a 400-portion batch is not the same as running one.

cards.title: The tryout picked a different chef than a tasting would.
body: The restaurant chef's sauce tasted best. But her batch drifted as it grew, and she guessed at the cost.
The banquet sous-chef hit the recipe spec, costed it to the cent and gave the two cooks a clear five-minute brief. Mira hired her.
**Testing real skills** worked because the test came straight from the role list. Each step checked one outcome Mira had written down.

image.label: Scorecard comparing two chefs on four outcomes
image.brief: 주방 벽에 붙은 점수표 인포그래픽. 행은 "Consistency", "Cost", "Team brief", "Food safety", 열은 "Chef A", "Chef B". B 열에 체크가 더 많고, A 열의 "Taste"에는 별표. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: A tryout is a sample, not the whole job.
body: Half a day can't show how someone leads through a bad month. Pair the tryout with the same structured questions for every finalist, and with references.

Give everyone the same task, scored against the list you wrote before meeting them. Keep it short and pay for the time. A long unpaid "trial" is free labor, and strong candidates often walk away. Rules on trial shifts differ by place, so check local norms.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: You sell scheduling software to clinics and need your first customer support lead. One finalist has a famous tech company on her résumé. Another has used your product for years at a clinic.

options.text: Hire the famous-company candidate after a good conversation
options.feedback: A big name says she did well somewhere else. Without a role definition, you don't know if that work looks like yours.

options.text: List the year-one outcomes, then give both a paid task: answer three real anonymized tickets and write one help article
options.feedback: **Defining the role** tells you what good looks like. **Testing real skills** shows who can do it with your real users and tickets.

options.text: Hire the long-time user because she knows the product
options.feedback: Product knowledge is a real head start. But knowing the product isn't the same as calming upset users or building a help center.

cards.title: Write the job down, then test the job.
body: Two concept lessons did the work here. **Defining the role** turned "a great chef" into four outcomes. **Testing real skills** checked those outcomes with a task taken from the real work.
**Try it today:** pick a role you may hire for next. Write four things it must deliver in year one. Then write one short task that would show each of them.
